Chapter 1: Regret Is Part of Being Human.
Regret—it's one of those feelings most of us would rather not talk about, right? Yet, it's every bit as real and natural as hope or joy. Sometimes, regret slips in quietly, just a faint ache in the background. Other times, it hits you hard, like a sharp pang you can't ignore.
Most people try to shove regret aside, maybe even pretend it isn't there. But if you take a closer look, regret actually says a lot about what truly matters to you.
Picture this: a woman in her late thirties, sitting alone at her kitchen table after her kids are asleep. She remembers a job offer she once had—a chance to move to a new city and start fresh. Back then, she picked stability over adventure, thinking it was best for her young family. Now, years later, she wonders... what if she’d taken that leap? The regret isn’t just about that job. It’s about all those paths she didn’t walk down, those possibilities she never explored.
And she’s not alone. No matter where you’re from or how old you are, everyone carries regrets. Some are tiny, just little nagging thoughts. Others? They change the course of your life. Maybe it’s a retired teacher who can’t forget a harsh word said to a student long ago. Or a recent grad who wishes he’d spoken up for a friend instead of staying silent. These moments sting, sure, but they’re not signs you’ve failed. They’re proof you care. They show you want to do better.
The truth is, regret is universal. If you ask almost anyone, they can name at least one thing they wish they’d done differently. Sometimes it’s about something they did—like words said in anger, or chances missed because of fear. Other times, it’s about what they didn’t do—the apology never spoken, the risk never taken.
What’s interesting is how often people try to bury these feelings. We hear it all the time: “No regrets.” As if moving forward means never looking back. But if you think about it, that attitude skips over something important. When you face regret honestly, it can actually help you grow.
Take a young man, frustrated with where his career is heading. He tells himself he has no regrets, but late at night, he can’t stop thinking about the time he dropped out of a promising program. The more he tries to brush off the feeling, the more it sticks around. Finally, he admits it—he wishes he’d made a different choice. And in that moment, the regret loses some of its sting. It starts to feel more like a guide, showing him what matters to him and what he wants to change.
Regret isn’t some problem you need to fix. It’s a signal—a reminder that your choices count. It pops up when something really important is at stake: relationships, your integrity, your dreams. So what if, instead of seeing regret as a burden, you saw it as a teacher? It asks tough questions, like "What do you care about?" or "What would you do differently next time?" In that way, regret isn’t the enemy of happiness. If anything, it’s a companion that helps you find a more meaningful life.
